answer: Pius X, of immortal memory, carefully prescribed the norms to be followed in sacred music in an Encyclical which begins with the words Tra le sollecitudini. Finally, We Ourselves, by Our Encyclical Mediator Dei, We have clearly pointed out the principles and norms to be followed in this matter, and We have briefly summarized them in these words: “Music is a part of the liturgy, and it has a share in the solemnity and splendor of the sacred ceremonies; its chief purpose is to add greater efficacy to the text, in order that through it the faithful may be the more easily moved to devotion and better disposed to receive the fruits of grace which come from the celebration of the sacred mysteries.”[[1]](#footnote-1) But for this reason music must possess the qualities proper to the liturgy, that is, holiness and goodness of form; from these two qualities its other character, universality, spontaneously derives.[[2]](#footnote-2) Thus it must be holy, and therefore avoid all profanity, not only in itself but also in the manner in which it is performed by those who execute it. It must also be true art, for otherwise it cannot have that effect on the minds of its hearers which the Church intends to achieve by admitting into her liturgy the art of musical sound. At the same time it must be universal, in the sense that, while each nation may admit into its compositions for religious purposes those special forms which may be said to constitute its native music, still these forms must be subordinated in such a way that they are not unsuited to the general character of the music used in the Church, so that no member of any other nation may be displeased on hearing it.[[3]](#footnote-3)
